source.title: Mapping Faithful Reasoning in Language Models
source.authors: Jia-Zheng Li; Andreas Damianou; J. Rosser; José Luis Redondo García; Konstantina Palla

record.file_problem: none; full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study uses a difference-of-means safety direction as a tool for analyzing reasoning activations, but does not report results testing whether ablating or adding the direction changes refusal or general capability.
record.gate_note: The paper describes selecting a direction using refusal-suppression, refusal-induction, and KL criteria, but reports no results for those selection metrics. The reported results concern projected activation trajectories during baseline and deliberately perturbed reasoning; these are recorded as findings about the related activation dynamics, not as tests of refusal mediation.
record.test_reason: The study uses an Arditi-style difference-in-means direction, selected by bypass, induce and KL criteria, only as a projection axis for tracing CoT activations in Qwen 3-4B. It reports no ablation, addition, refusal-rate or capability results. The direction-selection metrics are used to choose the axis and their values are never reported. The trajectory results concern CoT faithfulness, not whether the direction mediates refusal. The record's relation and tranche are correct.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that in hard cases perturbations cause sustained, structured shifts in internal safety activation, consistent with CoT-as-computation. In easy cases shifts are transient and the model reverts, consistent with decorative reasoning. They frame Concept Walk as a methodological contribution, with limitations: a direction learned in non-thinking mode, incomplete faithfulness filtering, and a single model.
record.recipe_differences: Uses a difference-of-means safety direction derived from safe and unsafe prompts, but projects it onto reasoning-step activations rather than reporting the original causal refusal ablation and addition tests. The direction is learned in non-thinking mode and used to analyze thinking-mode trajectories.
record.method_sensitivity: The safety direction is learned in non-thinking mode and applied to thinking-mode activations; trajectories are divided into hard and easy cases based on response sensitivity to injected CoT errors. The paper notes that perturbation timing and strength were not systematically varied.

fits_no_version.finding: In Qwen 3-4B thinking mode, injected flawed CoT steps produce sustained shifts in projected safety-direction cosine in 'hard' (output-flipping) cases. In 'easy' cases the shifts are transient and revert. Unsafe prompts show much higher initial projection than safe prompts. All results are figure-only.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Projection onto a refusal/safety direction tracks whether CoT perturbations are integrated into a reasoning model's decision (CoT faithfulness).

record.problems: No reported numerical results for the direction-selection refusal or KL metrics; activation-trajectory results are presented in figures without numerical values in the text. Only Qwen 3-4B is studied. The authors caution that filtered violative cohorts are small, that a non-thinking-mode direction may not fully represent thinking-mode activations, and that perturbation filtering does not guarantee complete CoT faithfulness.
record.rows_left_out: No reported results were left out. The paper's direction-selection criteria are described but have no reported outcomes, so they are not rows.

untested.parts: Ablation and addition effects on refusal, and capability retention. The direction is selected with these criteria (Appendix 7.1), but no results are reported.
Whether the direction mediates refusal in thinking mode. The direction is learned in non-thinking mode and only projected onto thinking-mode activations, with no intervention in thinking mode.
Transfer from non-thinking to thinking mode is assumed, not tested (Section 3.3, Limitations).
No separation of harm judgment from refusal. The authors only note the direction may partly encode refusal patterns.

record.verdict_notes: Appendix 7.1 asserts that the method shows refusal 'can be mediated by a single interpretable direction'. This restates Arditi et al.; the paper provides no results of its own supporting it. Only one model (Qwen 3-4B) is studied, and the datasets are synthetic music-playlist prompts generated by Mistral-7B. Arditi et al. (arXiv:2406.11717), the original source, is cited as the method source. No instructions were found in the text.

versions.untested_parts: No reported causal ablation or addition results measuring refusal and general capability.
No weight edit or released-model abliteration results.
No test of attacks suppressing the direction or training against its ablation.
No comparison of a single direction with affine, cone, or multiple-direction accounts.
No test separating harmfulness judgment from refusal decision.
No transfer test across languages, model variants, or base and instruct models.
No comparison of refusal-training procedures or stages for the existence of a removable direction.
The study analyzes a thinking model but does not test whether the causal refusal claim holds in reasoning models.
